data.body:
## Filed 0d6c: AGENTS.md's orphan-prevention guidance does not work on this platform

An agent leaked an orphaned zsh at PPID 1 burning 87% CPU tonight WHILE FOLLOWING the documented
guidance. It caught the leak itself with scripts/check_orphaned_load.py and killed it, so no harm --
but the prevention advice is what failed, and that section exists specifically to prevent the
documented incident where 38 processes orphaned and ran four days at ~1341% combined CPU.

TWO INDEPENDENT GAPS, both observed today:
 1. 'timeout' DOES NOT EXIST on this macOS host (no coreutils, no gtimeout). The documented primary
    bound returns 127 and the command you meant to bound NEVER RUNS -- a silent no-op that reads as
    success. I hit this myself earlier and only noticed because expected output was missing.
    'perl -e "alarm N; exec @ARGV" <cmd>' works.
 2. 'trap "kill 0" EXIT INT TERM' inside a SUBSHELL did not reap the wrapper. AGENTS.md presents it
    as signalling 'the entire process group, so it reaps helpers you forgot about' -- true only at the
    right scope, which the document does not state.

Why this is worth a ticket rather than a note: every subagent brief in this repo repeats that
guidance, so a gap propagates to every agent that spawns anything. Tonight it propagated to at least
one, which leaked exactly the class of process the section exists to prevent WHILE BELIEVING IT HAD
COMPLIED. Confident compliance with broken advice is worse than no advice.

Deliberately scoped OUT: wiring an orphan check into make lint. check_orphaned_load.py is excluded
from lint on purpose -- it reports on live HOST state rather than the tree under review, and that
reasoning is sound and documented. The detector works and is what caught this. The ticket is about
the PREVENTION advice only.

This is the same shape as the night's other findings, one level up again: the guidance ASSERTED a
property (bounded, reaped) that it did not deliver, and nothing surfaced the gap until a process was
already orphaned. 'What did not run' applied to a safety mechanism rather than a test.
